To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
RA patients have increased frequencies of intermediate monocytes that show specific and distinctive molecular profiles, associated to atherosclerotic plaques and to the increased CV risk.

the generation of monocyte subsets is associated to the auto-inflammatory response that drives RA, that these monocyte subsets display specific and distinctive signatures, and that these subsets promote endothelial dysfunction through a finely regulated mechanism, which in turn drives atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease development in RA.

RA patients have an increase in intermediate CD14++CD 16+ monocyte frequency and that this increase is associated to the presence of atherosclerosis, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation and CV risk in RA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the monocyte subpopulation involved in RA-associated CVD and their specific molecular signatures, which could be potential biomarkers and/or therapeutic targets.
the molecular characterization of monocyte subsets and their involvement in the development of CVD in RA.
the characterization of RA monocytes, and their implication in the increased CVD risk in RA patients, with the aim of identifying new targets and therapeutic strategies for RA treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RA monocyte subsets are associated with the increased CV risk in patients with RA.
RA patients display a proinflammatory monocyte profile associated to the disease, that is interrelated to atherosclerosis and CV risk.

the generation of intermediate monocytes is associated with the autoimmune/inflammatory process that mediates RA and these subsets, which display specific and distinctive functional features, might promote endothelial activation and dysfunction, in turn contributing to the progression of atheroma lesions and CVD development in this population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the increased frequency of inflammatory monocytes in RA is associated to the presence of a pro-atherogenic environment.
RA is a systemic inflammatory disease, and the inflammatory process that characterizes it is associated to an increased cardiovascular risk.
the generation of CD14++CD 16+ monocytes is associated with the autoimmune/inflammatory process in RA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
monocyte subpopulating in RA are not only increased in frequency but also display distinctive molecular and functional profiles, which might contribute to CVD development in this disease.
monocyte subsets in rheumatoid arthritis patients are not just a biomarker of the disease but also a key player in the pathogenesis of cardiovascular disease in these patients.
monocytes in RA patients have a specific and different molecular profile than those of HDs, and these differences may be associated with atheroma development and increased CV disease risk.
